$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -10 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ -8\end{aligned}]=\lambda [\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

This leads to the following system of equations for $\lambda :$

$$
{\begin{aligned}-10=5\lambda  \\ -8=2\lambda \end{aligned}
$$

This system has no solution. Therefore, $v$ is not an eigenvector of $A.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7db53a96-c2b8-5320-933c-98ee29c6736b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-7db53a96-c2b8-5320-933c-98ee29c6736b" :answer-field/id #uuid "7db53a96-c2b8-5320-933c-98ee29c6736b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-789dcf2a-206e-57f2-a9a3-9f05e8688d99" :answer-field/choices ["answer-15a7b8b4-79e0-5a5e-b815-4fb73d16b52a" "answer-b6451324-810e-5585-b20a-6b631b55ec25" "answer-eb0c0a14-6cf1-5cc9-93cf-929bd01a89bc" "answer-9f3222d4-dee2-5a55-8149-170c56576786" "answer-789dcf2a-206e-57f2-a9a3-9f05e8688d99"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-15a7b8b4-79e0-5a5e-b815-4fb73d16b52a" :answer/id #uuid "15a7b8b4-79e0-5a5e-b815-4fb73d16b52a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b6451324-810e-5585-b20a-6b631b55ec25" :answer/id #uuid "b6451324-810e-5585-b20a-6b631b55ec25" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-eb0c0a14-6cf1-5cc9-93cf-929bd01a89bc" :answer/id #uuid "eb0c0a14-6cf1-5cc9-93cf-929bd01a89bc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9f3222d4-dee2-5a55-8149-170c56576786" :answer/id #uuid "9f3222d4-dee2-5a55-8149-170c56576786" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-789dcf2a-206e-57f2-a9a3-9f05e8688d99" :answer/id #uuid "789dcf2a-206e-57f2-a9a3-9f05e8688d99" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$v$ is not an eigenvector of $A$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-0ddf6872-c9fc-59bb-a8a4-f3c287d11e0a" :question/id #uuid "0ddf6872-c9fc-59bb-a8a4-f3c287d11e0a" :question/math-academy-id "q-75724" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

- $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =1.$
- $v=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5.$
- If $v$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3,$ then $2v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda =-3.$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1v.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $Av=v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (but not $1$).

- Statement II is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A{v}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =-4\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-4{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $Av=-4v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-4$ (but not $5$).

- Statement III is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(2v)=2Av=2(-3v)=-3(2v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(2v)=-3(2v),$ and $2v\ne 0,$ this implies that $2v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-3.$

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only"." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e96c0df0-7687-56d8-909c-da1e58046f59"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e96c0df0-7687-56d8-909c-da1e58046f59" :answer-field/id #uuid "e96c0df0-7687-56d8-909c-da1e58046f59" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-5554e24d-43d6-558c-beb2-10fff427646c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-2add26dd-e43b-52c7-b2dd-74816713310b" "answer-4d09cdfe-9545-5f99-9a96-7ea92e64cc13" "answer-273db6e4-b799-50bd-a66c-30f726dc163b" "answer-5554e24d-43d6-558c-beb2-10fff427646c" "answer-a4868990-cd46-582c-81e2-72d1d4d50bee"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2add26dd-e43b-52c7-b2dd-74816713310b" :answer/id #uuid "2add26dd-e43b-52c7-b2dd-74816713310b" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4d09cdfe-9545-5f99-9a96-7ea92e64cc13" :answer/id #uuid "4d09cdfe-9545-5f99-9a96-7ea92e64cc13" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-273db6e4-b799-50bd-a66c-30f726dc163b" :answer/id #uuid "273db6e4-b799-50bd-a66c-30f726dc163b" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5554e24d-43d6-558c-beb2-10fff427646c" :answer/id #uuid "5554e24d-43d6-558c-beb2-10fff427646c" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a4868990-cd46-582c-81e2-72d1d4d50bee" :answer/id #uuid "a4868990-cd46-582c-81e2-72d1d4d50bee" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "None" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107090 :tutorial/content "Given a matrix $A,$ an **eigenvector** of $A$ is a *non-zero* vector $\mathbf{v}$ such that 

$$
A \mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v}
$$

for some scalar $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}.$ The scalar $\lambda$ is called the **eigenvalue** corresponding to the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}.$

For example, consider the matrix 
![](images/63/63e2c65a23a0680412a14084d543b6cc19c0529fd80863b09c99987d309eaa4f.svg) 
and the vector ![](images/b7/b7811b74d8d3075357925864b5be27f57b292dadca9c04d222954baa1e66ba2a.svg) Computing the product $A \cdot \mathbf{v},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =(-2)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =-2v.\end{aligned}
$$

We've discovered that $A {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}} = {\color{red}-2} {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}}.$ Therefore,

- the vector ![](images/13/13a28e543647ede7a88b30fb652bd7fba6c9adb8ee3142161a102de947ef2d2a.svg) is an *eigenvector* of $A,$ and

- the scalar $\color{red}\lambda=-2$ is the *eigenvalue* corresponding to the eigenvector ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}}.$

**Caution:** Remember that an eigenvector must be a *non-zero* vector. This is very important." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186106002 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$

 
Since $Av=v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-1$ (but not $1$).

$$
\begin{aligned}A{v}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =-4\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-4{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}A(2v)=2Av=2(-3v)=-3(2v).\end{aligned}

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

- If $v$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $5$ then $10v$ is also an eigenvector corresponding to $5.$
- $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $6.$
- $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ is an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $4.$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(10v)=10Av=10(5v)=5(10v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(10v)=5(10v),$ and $10v\ne 0,$ this implies that $10v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =5.$

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 18\end{aligned}] \\  & =6[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =6v.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Av=6v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =6.$

- Statement III is true. We have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =4v.\end{aligned}

[{:db/id 17592186106673 :step/content {:db/id 17592186107090 :tutorial/content "Given a matrix $A,$ an **eigenvector** of $A$ is a *non-zero* vector $\mathbf{v}$ such that 

$$
A \mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v}
$$

for some scalar $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}.$ The scalar $\lambda$ is called the **eigenvalue** corresponding to the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}.$

For example, consider the matrix 
$[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]$
